title: What happens to a class mean when two new students join?
description: A class of twenty four students has a mean height of one hundred and fifty point two centimetres, and two new students join. The new heights must be measured, the mean goes up because the extra above is more than the shortfall below, and the median cannot be told.
teaching_notes: One idea: the old mean and count give the old total, so only the new values are needed to update the mean, while the median needs the full sorted list. Watch for students who say the mean must rise just because the count rises.

source: Figure it Out (more on mean and median, question 6)
video_script.why: A child who has corrected a mean by changing the total now updates a mean when new values join.
video_script.substitution: the book's class of 24 students with mean height 150.2 cm and two new students of 149 cm and 152 cm
video_script.anchor: a line of twenty four students beside two new students, with the mean height 150.2 cm marked
video_script.payoff_line: The new heights must be measured, the mean increases, and the median cannot be told

final_answer.value: measure the new heights; the mean increases; the median cannot be told
final_answer.spoken: the new heights must be measured, the mean increases, and the median cannot be told

names.Laksh: class teacher who keeps the heights of the class

never_show: a statement that the median must increase or decrease, marked as right
maths_rules: 149 − 150.2 = −1.2 (below) and 152 − 150.2 = +1.8 (above); net +0.6, so the mean goes up
median depends on the sorted heights of all 26 students, which are not given, so not enough information
video_script.design: One line of students all video. Two new students step in, and a balance bar shows the shortfall below the old mean against the extra above it. The sorted line stays hidden for the median.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the mean and the median.
<bookmark mark='class'/>The class of Laksh has twenty four students. Their mean height is one hundred and fifty point two centimetres.
<bookmark mark='new'/>Two new students join the class. Their heights are one hundred and forty nine centimetres and one hundred and fifty two centimetres.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What happens to the mean, and what happens to the median?

beats.on_screen: total = mean × count; the median depends on where each value sits in the sorted list

narration: <bookmark mark='total'/>The mean times the count gives the total of the class.
<bookmark mark='median'/>A median depends on where each value sits in the sorted list.
<bookmark mark='hidden'/>The mean alone cannot tell us where the values sit.

<bookmark mark='net'/>The extra above is more than the shortfall below, so the mean goes up.

marks.up: 150.22 is shown to the right of 150.2 on a number line

narration: <bookmark mark='old'/>Check the mean with exact numbers. The old total is twenty four times one hundred and fifty point two.
<bookmark mark='tot'/>That is three thousand six hundred and four point eight.
<bookmark mark='new'/>Add the two new heights, which total three hundred and one. The new total is three thousand nine hundred and five point eight.
<bookmark mark='div'/>Divide by twenty six students to get about one hundred and fifty point two two.
<bookmark mark='up'/>That is above the old mean, so the mean did go up.
